newsitem.title: UK: Alzheimer's in third of old car driver victims.
newsitem.headline: Alzheimer's in third of old car driver victims.

text.p: Finnish and Swedish researchers reported on Friday they had found at least a third of older drivers killed in car accidents had Alzheimer's disease, and that many more had early symptoms of the illness.
They said their findings had strong implications for older drivers and urged them, as well as their doctors and relatives, to be on the lookout for symptoms of Alzheimer's.

Noting that older drivers have a higher risk of car accidents, Matti Viitanen and colleagues at Huddinge University Hospital in Sweden examined the brains of 98 drivers above the age of 65 who were killed in accidents in Finland and Sweden.
Thirty-three percent of them had the tangled nerves and brain "plaques" that mark Alzheimer's, which causes increasing forgetfulness, confusion and, eventually, death.
Another 20 percent indicated early stages of Alzheimer's, which is very hard to diagnose.
The researchers also found a genetic mutation associated with Alzheimer's, a certain version of a gene known as APOE, in more of the drivers who had been killed than in "control" samples.
"It is possible that 47 to 53 percent of drivers killed may have had incipient Alzheimer's disease," they wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal. The implications were clear, they said.
"It had been shown that people with mild Alzheimer's disease have impaired performance in traffic, and that those with dementia have more accidents than age-matched controls."
The accidents are mostly at intersections, where drivers have to think and process more information -- just the areas affected by Alzheimer's.

"Because of the insidious onset of Alzheimer's disease, affected people do not generally seek medical advice during the early stages, and if they do, the physician may not recognise early cognitive impairment," they added.
Therefore, they urged careful screening of elderly drivers.

"Older drivers involved in accidents should have their cognitive performances tested; and older drivers themselves, their relatives and physicians should be on the lookout for early symptoms of impaired cognition which would increase the risk of automobile accidents."

Alzheimer's affects two to three percent of people over 65 -- for example more than four million Americans. It is the world's fourth most common cause of death in later life, international figures show.
Simon Denegri of Britain's Alzheimer's Disease Society said driving and age was a sensitive area.
"Driving is seen very much as a sign of independence," he said. "It's quite a difficult issue for families and carers to deal with in order to persuade someone to give up driving."
But he pointed to new drugs and treatments that, while not a cure, help ease the symptoms in early Alzheimer's and could help patients drive safely for longer.
